title: Smooth real differentiation rules
statement:
Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field]. Let $E,F,G$ be finite-dimensional normed real vector spaces (finite-dimensional means spanned by finitely many vectors). On open subsets, smooth means $C^\infty$ in real coordinates and $Df$ is the real Frechet differential, a continuous real-linear map. Constants and continuous real-linear maps are smooth, with differentials zero and the map itself. Sums and compositions of smooth maps are smooth; products of smooth maps into $\mathbf R$ or $\mathbf C$ are smooth. A smooth map is differentiable, and its differential, as a map into continuous real-linear maps, is smooth. At points where the indicated differentials exist,
$$D(f+g)=Df+Dg,\qquad D(uv)(x)[v_0]=u(x)Dv(x)[v_0]+v(x)Du(x)[v_0],\qquad D(g\circ f)(x)=Dg(f(x))\circ Df(x).$$
In the product formula $u,v$ are scalar-valued and $v_0\in E$. The real function $t\mapsto\log t$ is smooth at every $t>0$ and has derivative $t^{-1}$ there.
